thread.title: Duke Libraries signs onto national statement of shared AI practice
thread.title_full: Duke Libraries signs onto national statement of shared AI practice

author: Seyun Park
title: Duke Libraries signs onto national statement of shared AI practice
text:
Duke University Libraries has signed on to a national “Statement of Shared Practice” on how to manage collection requests from artificial intelligence developers that seek to use information held in research libraries to train large language models.
Originally commissioned by the University of Virginia Library, the statement principally aims to prevent “archival, manuscript, rare and special collections” from being misused to train AI, by focusing on issues of ownership and provenance, a term for the origins of a document or object.
“The question before us is not whether to engage with AI, but on what terms, for what purposes and with what protections for the communities and collections we serve,” the statement says.
The agreement, described by the UVA Libraries as a framework “designed to protect the integrity of cultural heritage materials as AI developers increasingly seek access to them,” was announced in early April. Although Duke signed onto the statement, the agreement itself is non-binding, meaning the University still has the autonomy to make AI access deals.
“We wanted to be at the table as more people were talking about [AI],” said Joseph Salem, Rita DiGiallonardo Holloway University librarian and vice provost for Duke library affairs. Salem also serves as a co-chair on the AI at Duke Steering Committee which authored the University’s recent AI report.
“We're creating a bigger cohort of different institutions who really just want to get a sense of ‘What does the landscape look like?’ and ‘How do we do this ethically?” Salem said.
The two-page statement contains six main “shared commitments,” which include to “favor methods where source materials remain under institutional control” and “apply heightened scrutiny and a presumption against approval” of broad commercial training requests.
AI has increasingly played a larger role in libraries, ranging from digitization of library collections to training and education in classes.
However, generative AI models – once given access to a library’s collection – could lose the connection to the original owner and not correctly cite the original source. The tendency has made it increasingly important for libraries to track their collection ownership and manage AI model usage.
“What struck me was that the materials being requested are irreplaceable,” UVA Dean of Libraries Leo Lo said in an April 3 press release explaining the purpose of the statement.
“Unpublished letters, photographic archives, oral histories, manuscript drafts…That felt like something the archival community needed to address together, not one library at a time,” Lo continued.
Salem said Duke Libraries has been increasingly receiving requests from AI developers for access to their special collections, and that the statement provided a non-legally binding path to establish a more concrete method of processing those requests.
“We wanted to make sure that we had a framework to be able to respond to those requests systematically, thoughtfully and to make sure that it was all vetted the same way,” Salem said.
The University has not yet signed any access deals, but Salem suspects that much of DUL’s open-access materials available online have already been scraped by bots for AI training. DUL has since added an anti-bot tool to the back end of its catalog to prevent bot interference.
The Statement of Shared Practice calls for a confidential shared ledger among member universities that records requests received by libraries and tracks general terms of agreement and pricing.
Although universities are not required to contribute to the ledger, the agreement discourages signatories from signing agreements with AI developers that would prevent them from “category-level information sharing.”
The commitments in the statement are scheduled to run through April 2027, but the signatories will reconvene in February 2027 to discuss results and decide whether to extend, revise or conclude the agreement.
Ultimately, Salem hopes the statement will encourage library leaders to discuss AI and training requests “in a way that recognizes the moment and contributes to innovation, but without giving away our content irresponsibly.”
UVA Libraries said that more than 42 institutions contributed to the development of the Statement of Shared Practice, but the agreement was made official with 11 initial signatories. Besides Duke and UVA, the other signatories include the libraries of Florida State University, Northwestern University, Oklahoma State University, Rice University, Tulane University, the University of Florida, the University of Rochester, the University of Wisconsin-Madison, Washington University in St. Louis and Wayne State University.
